story.title: Trump Resumes Efforts to Dismiss Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook
story.summary: Donald Trump is renewing his attempts to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook after the US Supreme Court previously blocked his efforts. The administration is moving forward with the dismissal despite Cook's denial of mortgage fraud allegations that prompted the initial attempt to terminate her position.

explore_lenses.label: Why does Cook’s removal fight matter?
explore_lenses.title: A test of Fed independence and removal limits
explore_lenses.summary: The dispute concerns whether a president can remove a Federal Reserve governor before the end of a protected term, and what process is required before doing so.

claims.text: Federal Reserve governors serve staggered 14-year terms and may be removed by the president only “for cause”; Congress designed the terms to insulate the Board from day-to-day political pressure.
Cook’s current term is scheduled to end on January 31, 2038, rather than during the current presidential term.

The Supreme Court said accepting the administration’s prior position could turn the Fed’s statutory for-cause protection into at-will employment, contrary to Congress’s design and the tradition of central-bank independence.

The Supreme Court said accepting the administration’s prior position could turn the Fed’s statutory for-cause protection into at-will employment, contrary to Congress’s design and the tradition of central-bank independence.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The Court did not definitively define what conduct qualifies as “cause” for removing a Fed governor.

explore_lenses.label: How did the Cook dispute reach this point?
explore_lenses.title: A prior firing attempt failed on procedure
explore_lenses.summary: The White House’s new notice follows its August 2025 attempt to remove Cook, which courts blocked while the legality of the action was litigated.

claims.text: In August 2025, Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte accused Cook of mortgage fraud involving 2021 mortgage applications; the allegation concerned conduct before she joined the Fed Board.
Trump then purported to remove Cook, but she sued and a district court issued a preliminary injunction preventing the removal from taking effect.

On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court denied the government’s request to suspend that injunction, holding that Cook had not received the statutory procedural protections needed to dispute the charges before removal.
Cook’s lawyers characterize the mortgage allegations as baseless and argue that the removal effort would interfere with Federal Reserve independence.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the new White House notice?
explore_lenses.title: Cook has until August 26 to respond
explore_lenses.summary: The administration is attempting to supply the notice-and-response process the Supreme Court found missing from the first effort, but a new removal action would likely face renewed legal scrutiny.

claims.text: In the new letter, White House aide Dan Scavino said Trump was considering Cook’s removal and gave her until August 26, 2026, to respond to the mortgage-fraud allegations.
Cook’s lawyers have said they will challenge any attempt to remove her and maintain that there is no valid cause for dismissal.

Whether a revised process permits removal remains unresolved because the Supreme Court’s June ruling expressly did not decide the precise meaning of “cause” or the full scope of judicial review of a president’s determination.

story_report.summary: President Donald Trump is again pursuing the removal of Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, after the Supreme Court blocked an earlier attempt from taking effect. A new White House notice says Trump is considering her dismissal over mortgage-fraud allegations that Cook denies and gives her until Aug. 26, 2026, to respond. The renewed process does not itself remove Cook, but it sets up a further dispute over the statutory limits on presidential authority over the Fed.

sections.heading: Federal Reserve Removal Protections
sections.body: Federal Reserve governors hold staggered 14-year terms and can be removed by a president only “for cause,” a structure Congress designed to limit day-to-day political pressure on the Board. Cook’s current term is scheduled to run through Jan. 31, 2038. In its prior ruling, the Supreme Court said the administration’s position risked converting the statutory protection into at-will employment, contrary to Congress’s design and the tradition of central-bank independence.

sections.heading: Mortgage Allegations and Prior Case
sections.body: Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte accused Cook in August 2025 of mortgage fraud involving 2021 mortgage applications, before she joined the Fed Board. Trump subsequently purported to remove her, but Cook sued and a district court issued a preliminary injunction preventing the action from taking effect. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court declined to suspend that injunction, finding that Cook had not received statutory procedural protections to contest the charges before removal; her lawyers call the allegations baseless.

sections.heading: Cook Response and Legal Challenge
sections.body: Cook’s lawyers say they will challenge any removal attempt and argue there is no valid cause for dismissal. The new notice provides an opportunity for her to respond before any final decision is announced. A renewed dismissal effort could lead to further court action, with the legal dispute centering on whether the revised process and asserted grounds meet the statute’s requirements.

unresolved.text: The Supreme Court has not defined precisely what conduct constitutes “cause” to remove a Federal Reserve governor, or the full extent of judicial review of a president’s determination.
The mortgage-fraud allegations against Cook were not resolved in the Supreme Court’s removal decision.
It remains unknown whether Cook’s response will result in another attempted dismissal or further litigation.

The incident has been described as chaotic, with bystanders attempting to assist the victims.

related_stories.title: Teenager Commits Deadly Shooting at School After Killing Grandparents in Thailand
related_stories.summary: A 14-year-old boy in Thailand killed his grandparents before opening fire at Debsirin Nonthaburi School, resulting in at least eight deaths, including his own. The attack, which occurred just outside Bangkok, left more than 30 others injured. Authorities reported that the boy used a firearm belonging to his grandfather and fired a total of 26 rounds during the incident. The motive for the shooting remains unclear.

This testimony comes as seven healthcare professionals are on trial in Argentina, facing allegations of negligence that may have contributed to the football legend's passing.
